content: 1. Institutions responsible for the education and training of health professionals may adopt targeted admissions policies to enhance the ethnic and geographical diversity of their student body. This approach is compared to not using such targeted policies. 2. Health professional education and training institutions might consider implementing streamlined educational pathways or ladder programs to facilitate the career advancement of practicing health professionals. This is evaluated against the option of not employing such pathways or programs. 3. Inter-professional education involves health professional students and faculty from multiple disciplines learning with, from, and about each other in both theoretical and practical components of their curricula. Institutions are encouraged to consider integrating inter-professional education into undergraduate and postgraduate programs, as opposed to not implementing it. 4. National governments are advised to consider introducing accreditation systems for health professional education programs. Accreditation ensures that institutions or programs meet predetermined and agreed-upon standards, as opposed to not having such systems in place. 5. Governments may also introduce regulations, such as licensure and registration, to ensure the quality and relevance of care provided by health professionals. This is compared to the absence of such regulatory measures. 6. Continuous professional development (CPD) and in-service training should be implemented by health professional education institutions to address the evolving healthcare needs of their communities. This is contrasted with not implementing such training programs. 7. The concept of acceptability refers to the perception among stakeholders that a particular service, practice, or innovation is agreeable, satisfactory, or culturally appropriate. This should be assessed based on stakeholders' knowledge or direct experience with the intervention. 8. Accreditation is a formal quality assurance process where an institution or program is evaluated and approved by a legitimate body to meet specific standards. This can be conducted by external agencies or through self-accreditation, depending on the system in place. 9. Active participation involves a high level of engagement in planning and contributing to governance and policy formation within an institution. 10. Active recruitment refers to the process of generating a pool of potential applicants for health professional education programs, rather than passively waiting for applications. 11. Adjunct faculty are part-time or temporary instructors whose compensation is not equivalent to that of full-time contractual faculty. 12. Certification is a voluntary process where a profession establishes competency standards for its members, often serving as a protective measure for the public in the absence of state regulation. 13. Competencies encompass the essential knowledge, skills, abilities, and values required for effective health promotion practice. 14. Compulsory service mandates health workers to serve in underserved or remote areas for a specified period, ensuring healthcare availability in these regions. 15. Continuing professional development (CPD) extends beyond clinical updates to include research, scientific writing, leadership, communication, and other multidisciplinary skills necessary for improved patient care and professional growth. 16. A core curriculum is a mandatory course of study central to all students within an educational institution. 17. Direct admission systems allow individuals with relevant prior learning experiences to transition into advanced levels of health professional education without redundancy. 18. Feasibility assesses whether a program or intervention can be successfully implemented under specific conditions, considering factors like cost, resources, and organizational rules. 19. Financial assistance includes all forms of monetary aid provided to students, such as grants, loans, scholarships, and tax credits, to support their education. 20. Governance refers to the structures and processes through which institutional decisions are made collectively, encompassing both operational and objective-related decisions. 21. Infrastructure in health education includes the physical spaces and resources necessary for learning activities, such as laboratories, lecture halls, and instrument rooms. 22. In-service training equips health workers with the skills needed to deliver specific interventions while they are fully employed in the health sector. 23. Inter-professional education fosters collaboration and improved health outcomes by engaging students and faculty from multiple health professions in shared learning experiences. 24. Joint appointments formalize agreements where an individual holds positions in two institutions, fulfilling defined responsibilities in both. 25. Ladder programs provide structured pathways for career advancement through graded steps or levels based on achievement. 26. Licensure is a government-regulated process that determines the competency of individuals to practice in specific professions, granting them the authority to do so. 27. Research capacity refers to the collective ability of education faculty to conduct independent or interdisciplinary research. 28. Results-based financing involves conditional payments or transfers made to governments, managers, or providers after achieving and verifying predefined outcomes. 29. Retention in education refers to maintaining a student's satisfactory progress toward their educational objectives until completion. 30. Return-of-service commitments require health workers to serve in underserved areas for a specified period in exchange for financial or in-kind incentives. 31. Rural populations are defined as those living in non-urban areas, with varying definitions based on factors like population density, distance from urban centers, and access to healthcare. 32. Scope of practice defines the activities a health professional is authorized to perform, influencing their ability to seek reimbursement for services. 33. Streamlined educational pathways connect education, training, and support services to prepare students for successive levels of education, avoiding redundancy in coursework. 34. Targeted admission policies reserve places in limited-entry programs for underrepresented or disadvantaged groups, promoting equal educational opportunities. 35. Trans-professional education involves health professionals learning alongside non-professional health workers, administrators, policymakers, and community leaders to foster collaboration and break down professional silos. 36. Twinning establishes formal links between institutions in developed and developing countries to share resources and expertise. 37. Underrepresented populations in healthcare professions are racial or ethnic groups whose representation is disproportionately low compared to their numbers in the general population. 38. Underserved populations are those with limited access to qualified healthcare providers and services, often residing in remote, rural, or conflict-affected areas. 39. WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for health interventions, addressing clinical, public health, or policy-related issues. These guidelines are developed through systematic reviews, stakeholder surveys, and expert group meetings to ensure feasibility and acceptability.
